text.arabic_uthmani: وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ ذَرُونِىٓ أَقْتُلْ مُوسَىٰ وَلْيَدْعُ رَبَّهُۥٓ ۖ إِنِّىٓ أَخَافُ أَن يُبَدِّلَ دِينَكُمْ أَوْ أَن يُظْهِرَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ٱلْفَسَادَ

words.gloss_range: opening conjunction/resumption that connects Pharaoh's speech to the prior conflict
words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) makes Pharaoh's statement a continuation of the conflict, not an isolated policy thought. The prefixed connector lets the quote enter as the next escalation after the prior verdict on scheming, while the clipped opening moves quickly into the reporting verb.

topics.headline: connected launch into royal speech
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears Pharaoh's proposal as an escalation within an ongoing narrative frame rather than as a fresh scene.
topics.reason: QAC marks an opening conjunction, and the CRITICAL rows converge on resumption before the speech report.

topics.headline: brief connector fused to speech frame
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the smallest word carries both linkage and a quick auditory release into declaration.
topics.reason: The rows describe the written prefixed form and its clipped-to-open cadence as part of the ayah opening.

words.gloss_range: perfect speech verb introducing Pharaoh's direct quote and its rationale
words.root_gloss_range: saying, declaring, and articulated claim; locally a completed public utterance, not negotiation
words.prose: {{ar:قَالَ}} ({{tr:qāla}}) makes language the first act of the ayah: Pharaoh stages killing as quoted public policy. The perfect speech verb governs the commands and fear-claims that follow, so the reader keeps the whole rationale inside Pharaoh's mouth rather than treating it as narrator judgment. Its simple Form I declaration is unilateral, and the same speech root opens a contested exchange that Moses answers in 40:27.

topics.headline: quoted speech contains the threat
topics.reader_payoff: The reader keeps the killing plan and the fear rationale inside reported royal speech, not neutral narration.
topics.reason: The perfect speech verb introduces the full direct quote according to QAC and attachment evidence.

topics.headline: speech as unilateral policy act
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Pharaoh converting intent into public authorization rather than entering counsel or reciprocal debate.
topics.reason: The speech-root rows and Form I rows support public assertion while blocking reciprocal negotiation morphology.

topics.headline: speech opens an answerable exchange
topics.reader_payoff: The reader expects Pharaoh's framing to be answered, especially by the next saying in 40:27.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows cite same-surah speech recurrence and the immediate answer in 40:27.

words.gloss_range: foreign proper royal name as nominative speaker-subject
words.prose: {{ar:فِرْعَوْنُ}} ({{tr:firʿawnu}}) names the speaker as the responsible royal actor before any command is issued. As a foreign proper title, it concentrates regime power without inviting an Arabic root image. The name also stands opposite the later possessed Lord-title, so the speech begins with royal sovereignty and soon exposes a rival authority relation, recalling Pharaoh's lordship claim in 79:24.

topics.headline: named ruler bears responsibility
topics.reader_payoff: The reader cannot detach the killing proposal from the named sovereign who voices it.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence makes the proper name the subject of the speech verb.

topics.headline: foreign title concentrates regime identity
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears more than a private individual; the title carries the recognizable regime figure into the grammar.
topics.reason: QAC treats the word as a foreign proper noun, and CRITICAL rows frame it as regime-name rather than Arabic-root derivation.

topics.headline: royal name faces Lord-relation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the named ruler's authority is set against the Lord-relation Pharaoh later mentions, with 79:24 sharpening the contrast.
topics.reason: The intertext rows explicitly connect Pharaoh-name with the Lordship field and cite 79:24.

words.gloss_range: plural imperative with first-person object suffix, asking a group to leave Pharaoh unrestrained
words.root_gloss_range: leaving, abandoning, letting be, and permitting; locally narrowed to demanded noninterference
words.prose: {{ar:ذَرُونِىٓ}} ({{tr:dharūnī}}) makes Pharaoh's audience grammatically responsible for noninterference: a plural command releases a first-person object from restraint. The leaving-root lets the demand sound like being left alone, but the next verb reveals that this permission enables killing. The fuller suffix variant keeps Pharaoh's self-reference audible while the command distributes complicity outward.

topics.headline: plural audience commanded to release Pharaoh
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that Pharaoh first needs others to step back; noninterference is made into a commanded action.
topics.reason: QAC identifies a plural imperative with first-person object suffix, and attachment evidence treats the suffix as direct object.

topics.headline: leaving-root recoded as permission
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the political move: abandonment language becomes permission for violence, while local syntax keeps the sense at noninterference.
topics.reason: The root supports leaving and abandoning, but the imperative plus object suffix locally narrows it to a demand to be left unrestrained.

topics.headline: permission immediately enables killing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the hidden consequence of “leave me”: the audience is implicated before the victim is named.
topics.reason: The following jussive result clause makes the killing depend on the commanded noninterference.

topics.headline: suffix and sound keep Pharaoh centered
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears Pharaoh's self-positioning linger at the permission point without changing the grammar.
topics.reason: The variant opens the final first-person suffix while preserving the same syntax.

words.gloss_range: first-person jussive result/purpose verb naming Pharaoh's intended killing of Moses
words.root_gloss_range: killing and lethal removal; locally one-way targeted killing, not mutual combat
words.prose: {{ar:أَقْتُلْ}} ({{tr:ʾaqtul}}) is not an independent future plan; as a jussive result it is what Pharaoh wants the audience's noninterference to make possible. Its first-person Form I keeps Pharaoh himself as the killer, and the following proper name narrows violence to targeted assassination rather than combat. The root also reaches back to the plural killing policy in 40:25 and forward to the believer's objection in 40:28, making rhetoric the doorway to bloodshed.

topics.headline: killing depends on commanded noninterference
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees killing as the grammatical consequence of the audience's compliance, not a freestanding aside.
topics.reason: QAC and CRITICAL rows identify the verb as jussive after the imperative chain.

topics.headline: Pharaoh claims direct targeted killing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices both agency and asymmetry: Pharaoh says he will kill one named target, not fight a mutual battle.
topics.reason: The first-person verb and Moses as direct object select one-way targeted killing.

topics.headline: local killing motif intensifies
topics.reader_payoff: The reader tracks the shift from collective repression in 40:25 to Pharaoh's singular assassination intent and its answer in 40:28.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows cite the same-surah sequence and the root recurrence around 40:25, 40:26, and 40:28.

words.gloss_range: foreign proper name as direct object of the killing verb
words.prose: {{ar:مُوسَىٰ}} ({{tr:mūsā}}) receives the killing verb as a named object, so the threat is no longer abstract policy. Pharaoh names him without a messenger-title, reducing him in the speech to a removable person, while the larger Moses story and the coming Lord-reference keep his mission identity active. The name arrives after the lethal verb, making the listener hear the act before the target is disclosed.

topics.headline: proper name fixes the threatened body
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the regime's violence narrowed onto one named person.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence identifies Moses as the direct object of the killing verb.

topics.headline: identity named without honorific
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices Pharaoh's reduction of Moses to a killable individual even though the broader narrative preserves his envoy identity.
topics.reason: QAC treats the word as a foreign proper noun, and CRITICAL rows note the absence of an envoy-title.

topics.headline: target remains tied to invoked authority
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the object of killing remains the antecedent of the Lord-relation Pharaoh cannot erase, with 20:47 as contrast.
topics.reason: The rows connect the named target to the later possessed Lord-title and cite 20:47.

topics.headline: target revealed after lethal action
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the word order: killing lands first, then the named messenger-target.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows specifically mark the post-verbal position of the proper name.

words.gloss_range: connector before the third-person command clause, joining invocation to the killing proposal
words.prose: The second {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) binds Moses' invocation clause to the murder proposal rather than letting it stand outside the threat. Its coordination can feel concessive as well as additive: Pharaoh says, in effect, let him call, while treating that call as powerless inside the same royal speech.

topics.headline: invocation joined to the killing scene
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears Moses' appeal staged inside the same threat-frame, not as a detached devotional aside.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence coordinates the jussive invocation clause with the killing clause.

topics.headline: coordination doubles as dismissive challenge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices Pharaoh's contempt: the connector lets permission to call function as mockery after permission to kill.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows describe both additive and circumstantial/concessive force in context.

words.gloss_range: jussive command particle turning the following imperfect into a permitted or dared action
words.prose: {{ar:لْ}} ({{tr:l}}) turns the following call into a third-person jussive command or permission inside Pharaoh's speech. The particle makes Moses' invocation grammatically dependent before the Lord-object is even named, so Pharaoh theatrically permits the appeal while minimizing its force.

topics.headline: particle makes a third-person command
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that Moses' call is staged by Pharaoh as “let him call,” not simply narrated as an independent act.
topics.reason: QAC identifies the lām as governing a jussive verb.

topics.headline: permission becomes a dare
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the permission as a challenge placed between murder intent and invocation.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows qualify the command force as permissive and polemical in this setting.

words.gloss_range: jussive Form I call/invoke verb governed by the command particle
words.root_gloss_range: calling, summoning, inviting, and supplicating; the Lord-object selects invocation while preserving appeal beyond court control
words.prose: {{ar:يَدْعُ}} ({{tr:yadʿu}}) remains shortened under the command particle, so Moses' call is framed by Pharaoh's dare. Yet the verb's call-and-invocation range, completed by the Lord-object, gives Moses an appeal-channel outside the court's power. Placed after the killing proposal, the call is staged as powerless by Pharaoh, but the same root becomes part of Surah 40's larger argument over whom one calls.

topics.headline: jussive call remains under Pharaoh's staging
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Moses still grammatically active as caller, but inside a dare controlled by Pharaoh's wording.
topics.reason: The verb is governed by the jussive particle and its hidden subject refers back to Moses.

topics.headline: call range selects invocation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the word can mean call or summons, but the Lord-object narrows it to invocation while preserving an authority channel beyond Pharaoh.
topics.reason: The root range is broad, but the direct object is the possessed Lord-title, selecting invocation rather than claim-making derivatives.

topics.headline: dismissed call enters wider calling debate
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Pharaoh's permitted call as part of a broader calling-to-Lord pattern, including 7:134.
topics.reason: The intertext rows cite 7:134 and same-surah recurrence of calling language.

words.gloss_range: possessed singular Lord-title as object of invocation
words.root_gloss_range: mastery, sustaining, rearing, ownership, and governing authority; locally a specific Lord-relation attached to Moses
words.prose: {{ar:رَبَّهُۥٓ}} ({{tr:rabbahu}}) makes the invoked authority specific through Moses' possessive relation, not through Pharaoh's recognition. The root range brings governing, sustaining, owning, and nurturing authority into the title, while the singular suffix keeps that relation attached to the threatened target. Positioned before the emphatic first-person self-claim, it means Pharaoh's security argument starts immediately after he has named an authority outside his sovereignty; the next ayah answers this slot when Moses speaks of his Lord in 40:27.

topics.headline: suffix specifies Moses' Lord
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the invoked authority tied to Moses, not to Pharaoh or the court.
topics.reason: The possessed noun is the direct object of the call, and the suffix refers to Moses.

topics.headline: governing and sustaining authority
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears more than a bare title: the word carries sustaining authority, while the local possessive keeps it as Moses' specific Lord-relation.
topics.reason: The lexical range supports master, owner, nurturer, and authority, narrowed by the singular possessed local form.

topics.headline: his Lord versus your order
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the speech moving from Moses' vertical Lord-relation to the audience's possessed social order.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows connect Pharaoh-name with the Lordship field and contrast this possessive with the later audience possessive.

topics.headline: dismissed Lord becomes answer source
topics.reader_payoff: The reader expects the dismissed authority to return, and 40:27 immediately supplies that answer.
topics.reason: The rows cite the next-ayah Lord refuge and the broader Lordship dispute, including 26:23-24.

words.gloss_range: emphatic first-person particle shifting from command to claimed motive
words.prose: {{ar:إِنِّىٓ}} ({{tr:innī}}) turns Pharaoh's quote from commands into emphatic self-justification. The particle and first-person suffix fuse confirmation to royal self-reference, making his fear sound like public evidence. The opened suffix variant heightens that self-display without changing syntax, and the boundary is pointed: his anxious claim appears under the previous verdict against scheming.

topics.headline: emphasis turns threat into motive claim
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears Pharaoh recast a murder proposal as an asserted motive and risk assessment.
topics.reason: QAC marks the emphatic particle with first-person suffix before the fear predicate.

topics.headline: first-person suffix keeps Pharaoh centered
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices Pharaoh pulling attention back to himself at the moment he justifies violence.
topics.reason: The qirāʾah row opens the final suffix more fully while preserving the same first-person assertion.

topics.headline: self-justification follows judgment on scheming
topics.reader_payoff: The reader reads Pharaoh's fear claim under the prior narrative evaluation, not as transparent truth.
topics.reason: The boundary row links the transition from external verdict to Pharaoh's emphatic motive claim.

words.gloss_range: first-person imperfect fear verb governing projected threat clauses
words.root_gloss_range: fear, dread, and danger-awareness; locally claimed apprehension used as public rationale
words.prose: {{ar:أَخَافُ}} ({{tr:ʾakhāfu}}) governs two projected clauses, so Pharaoh kills on alleged futures, not on completed acts by Moses. The Form I wording presents him as the one who fears, while the wider root field exposes how fear can become political risk-language. That fear is later contested in 40:30, where a believer redirects fear toward judgment rather than regime stability.

topics.headline: fear governs possible futures
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that Pharaoh's stated grounds are projected dangers, not demonstrated crimes.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence makes both following subordinator clauses complements of the fear verb.

topics.headline: fear recasts aggression as precaution
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Pharaoh posing as endangered while the lexical field reveals fear as a tool of political justification.
topics.reason: The root range includes fear and danger-awareness, but the local Form I presents felt apprehension rather than causative frightening.

topics.headline: fear will be reoriented in 40:30
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that Pharaoh's fear is not the surah's final standard for danger; 40:30 contests it.
topics.reason: The rows explicitly cite the repeated fear language in 40:30.

topics.headline: fear redirects rival authority into accusation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the rhetorical pivot: after naming Moses' Lord, Pharaoh turns that rival authority into a security danger.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows mark the position after the possessed Lord-title.

words.gloss_range: first subordinator introducing the projected replacement branch
words.prose: The first {{ar:أَن}} ({{tr:ʾan}}) makes the replacement claim a feared proposition under Pharaoh's fear verb, not an asserted fact. It governs the subjunctive verb tightly and opens the first threat branch; its later repetition gives the fear clause a matched two-branch cadence.

topics.headline: first subordinator makes allegation projected
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the change-of-order claim as Pharaoh's feared content, not as a narrator-certified event.
topics.reason: QAC marks the particle as subjunctive governor before the first projected verb.

topics.headline: short subordinator launches matched branch form
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the first danger as part of an ordered branch structure that will be mirrored later.
topics.reason: The rows describe complementizer/nominalizing force and repeated cadence before both projected verbs.

words.gloss_range: Form II subjunctive verb for active alteration or replacement under fear
words.root_gloss_range: replacement, exchange, and transformation; locally active transformation of the audience's binding order
words.prose: {{ar:يُبَدِّلَ}} ({{tr:yubaddila}}) is subjunctive fear-content, so the alleged replacement remains projected. Its Form II shape makes the charge active and transformative: Pharaoh frames Moses as one who would make the audience's order other than itself. The root's replacement field is locally sharpened by the following possessed object, while the branch position makes this internal-order accusation the first danger before the speech widens to public corruption; 2:59 supplies a contrast where wrongdoers change a word.

topics.headline: subjunctive projected agency
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Pharaoh assigning agency to Moses while the grammar still marks the claim as feared projection.
topics.reason: The subjunctive verb follows the subordinator, and the hidden subject points back to Moses.

topics.headline: Form II makes replacement active
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the substitution image as active transformation of an existing order, while other derivational branches are not locally selected.
topics.reason: The root field includes exchange and substitution, but the local Form II selects active alteration.

topics.headline: replacement targets possessed order
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the marked pairing of replacement-language with the audience's binding order, with 2:59 as an alteration contrast.
topics.reason: The rows cite the replacement-plus-order pairing and the 2:59 alteration scene.

topics.headline: first threat branch before expansion
topics.reader_payoff: The reader tracks Pharaoh's rhetoric expanding from internal allegiance to a broader public-security accusation.
topics.reason: The verb occurs before the branch particle and is parallel to the later manifestation verb.

words.gloss_range: possessed abstract noun as the object Pharaoh says could be replaced
words.root_gloss_range: religion, judgment, obedience, obligation, recompense, and social order; locally politicized as the audience's shared order
words.prose: {{ar:دِينَكُمْ}} ({{tr:dīnakum}}) is the object Pharaoh says Moses may replace, and the plural suffix turns Pharaoh's fear into the audience's emergency. The word's range spans religion, judgment, obedience, and social order, so the accusation can sound both cultic and political. Its singular noun with plural possession makes one shared order belong to many, and the possessive shift from Moses' Lord to “your order” recodes vertical allegiance as group danger; 109:6 shows the possessive formula in a separation context that Pharaoh weaponizes here.

topics.headline: audience's order made replaceable
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Pharaoh move his personal fear onto the audience by making their possessed order the threatened object.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence makes the word the direct object of the replacement verb, with a plural possessive suffix.

topics.headline: religion and social order both live
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the threat is not only private belief; the word can carry judgment, obedience, obligation, and communal order.
topics.reason: The lexical rows support a broad obligation/judgment range, narrowed locally by possession and object position.

topics.headline: one shared order assigned to many
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the audience collectivized around one possessed order before the branch shifts.
topics.reason: The singular abstract noun plus plural suffix is the row's main form-specific payoff.

topics.headline: his Lord becomes your order
topics.reader_payoff: The reader tracks the possessive shift from Moses' Lord to the audience's order, with 109:6 showing a different use of “your religion” language.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows cite the possessive shift and 109:6.

words.gloss_range: disjunctive hinge between two projected threats, with variant pressure toward accumulation
words.prose: {{ar:أَوْ}} ({{tr:aw}}) is the hinge between the two feared outcomes. In the base wording it divides replacement of the audience's order from manifestation of corruption as alternative branches, while variant evidence can make them cumulative. Its rounded hinge also differs from the variant conjunction, so the audible pivot changes with the parse. The particle therefore exposes Pharaoh's accusation as rhetorically adjustable and widens the scene from possessed communal order to the public land-domain.

topics.headline: disjunction divides two threats
topics.reader_payoff: The reader tracks a turn from internal order to public territory through a single branch particle.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence coordinates the two projected clauses, and the particle marks their relation.

topics.headline: variant shifts alternative to cumulative
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the accusation can grammatically flex between either-or and both-and without losing its threat vocabulary.
topics.reason: The accepted variant evidence changes the branch relation but does not replace the base local parse.

topics.headline: rounded hinge changes with variant
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the pivot as well as parses it: the branch sound changes when the relation changes.
topics.reason: The row explicitly ties sound to the branch hinge and the expansion from order to land.

words.gloss_range: second subordinator making the final threat branch parallel to the first
words.prose: The second {{ar:أَن}} ({{tr:ʾan}}) keeps the corruption branch under Pharaoh's fear verb and makes it syntactically parallel to the first projected branch. Variant pressure can suppress or fold this marker, so the retained form matters: it prevents the final accusation from becoming a loose afterthought and gives both threats the same compact subordinator-plus-verb profile.

topics.headline: second subordinator equalizes branches
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the land-corruption claim as a co-ranked feared content, not a stray consequence.
topics.reason: The second subordinator governs the final subjunctive verb and coordinates with the first branch.

topics.headline: repeated marker is a marked base surface
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the repeated marker clarifies branch symmetry, while variants show that this surface need not have been explicit.
topics.reason: Variant evidence can reduce the marker, but the base wording keeps it before the second verb.

words.gloss_range: Form IV subjunctive verb for causing corruption to appear or prevail in the base reading
words.root_gloss_range: appearance, outwardness, surfacing, support, and prevailing; locally public manifestation with agency qualified by variant readings
words.prose: {{ar:يُظْهِرَ}} ({{tr:yuẓhira}}) remains subjunctive projected speech, so the final danger is Pharaoh's accusation rather than observed reality. In the base Form IV reading, Moses is framed as causing corruption to surface or prevail; the root's outwardness image makes hidden disorder become public. Accepted variants can shift agency toward corruption's own emergence or a passive profile, so the accusation's grammar is unstable even as the public-visibility vocabulary remains. The phrasing recalls corruption appearing in 30:41 and closes the quote on a territorial public frame.

topics.headline: subjunctive final danger remains projected
topics.reader_payoff: The reader keeps the final public-danger claim inside Pharaoh's feared projection.
topics.reason: QAC marks the verb as subjunctive under the second subordinator and attachment evidence places it in the second feared clause.

topics.headline: Form IV causes public surfacing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the charge as making corruption visible or dominant in public, while the root range is narrowed to the local manifestation frame.
topics.reason: The root supports appearance and prevailing; the base Form IV makes that visibility causative.

topics.headline: variant readings shift agency
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that Moses' direct agency can weaken under variants even though the accusation vocabulary persists.
topics.reason: Accepted variants make corruption subject or passive subject, so they qualify but do not replace the base parse.

topics.headline: public surfacing recalls 30:41
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears Pharaoh borrowing a recognizable surfacing-of-corruption frame, especially 30:41, for his accusation against Moses.
topics.reason: The intertext rows cite 30:41 and nearby same-root recurrence in 40:29.

words.gloss_range: preposition marking the land as domain where corruption is imagined to appear
words.prose: {{ar:فِى}} ({{tr:fī}}) supplies the spatial and domain frame for the final accusation. It makes the land the arena where corruption is imagined to appear, so the charge is no longer a bare abstraction. After the audience's possessed order, the preposition expands the fear rhetoric into public territory through one compact function word.

topics.headline: preposition makes land the manifestation domain
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees corruption located in a public arena rather than left as an unplaced abstraction.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence makes the following land noun the prepositional complement of this word.

topics.headline: one preposition expands accusation to public field
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the shift from communal order to broader land-domain.
topics.reason: The rows describe literal location and abstract domain converging in the final threat.

topics.headline: short form tightens final phrase
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears a brief function word binding the final territorial phrase into a tight accusation.
topics.reason: The rows emphasize the single-letter form and its smooth binding into the following noun.

words.gloss_range: definite genitive land-domain governed by the preposition
words.root_gloss_range: ground, land, territory, and earth; locally the public territorial arena of the accusation
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْأَرْضِ}} ({{tr:al-arḍi}}) is genitive after the preposition, so the land is the domain of manifestation rather than the direct object of Moses' action. Its definite singular form lets Pharaoh present a known, totalized public space as threatened. The root range runs from ground to territory to earth, magnifying the claim from internal order to world-like disorder, while the land-corruption pairing recalls 30:41 and contrasts with 40:29, where the same land becomes the stage of temporary dominion before divine judgment.

topics.headline: known land-domain under the preposition
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the land as the recognized arena of the accusation, not the thing Moses directly acts upon.
topics.reason: QAC marks the noun genitive after the preposition, and rows stress its definite recognized domain.

topics.headline: ground image magnifies public anxiety
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the claim grounded physically and scaled politically, while local grammar keeps it as the prepositional domain.
topics.reason: The root range covers ground, land, territory, and earth, narrowed by the local prepositional phrase.

topics.headline: familiar disorder frame borrowed
topics.reader_payoff: The reader recognizes Pharaoh borrowing land-corruption language, especially 30:41, while his proposed killing exposes reversal.
topics.reason: The rows cite 30:41 and the strong land-plus-corruption field.

topics.headline: land motif becomes royal anxiety
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the land motif moving from divine judgment and dominion frames into Pharaoh's propaganda, including the contrast with 40:29.
topics.reason: The rows cite 40:29 and same-surah land recurrence.

words.gloss_range: definite verbal noun as the final object/label of the accusation in the base reading
words.root_gloss_range: spoilage, unsoundness, corruption, and systemic disorder; locally the charged closing label Pharaoh attaches to Moses
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْفَسَادَ}} ({{tr:al-fasāda}}) closes Pharaoh's quote with a definite, morally loaded label. In the base reading it is the accusative object of the manifestation verb, so Pharaoh grammatically makes corruption something Moses would cause to appear, while the verbal-noun form keeps the charge abstract rather than naming a specific corruptor. The root's spoilage and unsoundness image turns politics into decay language. The irony is local and sharp: the quote ends by fearing corruption after Pharaoh has just voiced the killing verb, echoing patterns like 2:11 where corruption-language reverses onto its speakers.

topics.headline: final object becomes recognized evil label
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Pharaoh end with a shared public evil category while the base grammar assigns Moses causal display.
topics.reason: QAC marks the word accusative as object of the manifestation verb in the base reading, with definite article.

topics.headline: spoilage image sharpens the charge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels corruption as decay and unsoundness, while local form keeps it as the abstract charged label.
topics.reason: The root range supports spoilage and disorder; the local definite verbal noun selects the abstract process/state.

topics.headline: abstract process rather than named doer
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that Pharaoh closes on the evil category while managing agency through the prior verb.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL rows identify a definite verbal noun rather than an active participle.

topics.headline: corruption label rebounds on proposed killing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader catches the moral reversal: the ruler claims to fear corruption while proposing the corruptive act of killing.
topics.reason: The rows connect the final label with the earlier killing verb and cite the reversal pressure.

topics.headline: formulaic final landing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the final word as a charged closing formula, with 2:11 sharpening the reversal.
topics.reason: The rows cite 2:11, the land-corruption formula field, and the final sound/position.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: أقتل موسى ... أخاف أن يبدل دينكم أو أن يظهر في الأرض الفساد
baseline_models.mechanism: Pharaoh converts a proposed killing into preventive policy: remove the person before either replacement of the community's governing allegiance or the public emergence and prevalence of disorder.

activation_trace.role: Literal taking of life supplies the coercive intervention presented as prevention.
Expectation of a marked harm supplies the anticipatory logic for acting before evidence matures.
One thing standing in another's place makes replacement, not mere criticism, the first alleged danger.
Obedience and submission make din the community's practiced allegiance as well as its creed.
Rising into dominance gives the second danger a political sense of disorder becoming prevalent.
Departure from soundness supplies the adverse condition Pharaoh claims to forestall.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh simply threatens to kill Moses.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh frames lethal removal as anticipatory state protection against a transfer of allegiance or the public dominance of disorder.

baseline_models.mechanism: The possessives set rival jurisdictions against each other: Moses has a Lord, while the audience has a din whose branches include obedience, domination, customary order, and the city organized by authority.

activation_trace.role: Lordship as mastery and sovereignty supplies the rival authority named as Moses's.
Substitution makes the feared event a transfer from one authority relation to another.
Subjugation and rule expose the coercive political dimension inside 'your din.'
Habit and established practice make the threatened object a lived social order.
The city of obedience gives the possessive din a civic and institutional scope.

changed_reading.before: Moses might change the people's religious beliefs.
changed_reading.after: Moses threatens to transfer obedience and public jurisdiction away from Pharaoh's civic-religious order toward another Lord.

baseline_models.mechanism: The clause can carry two live directions: Moses may make disorder prevail, but he may also make an already present failure visible on the land's public surface. Pharaoh's wording does not identify whether Moses originates or exposes it.

activation_trace.role: Emergence and disclosure supply the possibility that the act is revelation rather than production.
Ascendancy and prevalence preserve the competing reading that disorder is made dominant.
The terrestrial domain supplies the public field in which either disclosure or prevalence occurs.
Loss of soundness names the condition whose source Pharaoh leaves strategically unspecified.

changed_reading.before: Moses will introduce corruption into the land.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh alleges either that Moses will make disorder dominant or that he will bring a corrupt condition into public visibility; the causation remains rhetorically underdetermined.

baseline_models.mechanism: Two permissive imperatives stage an efficacy contest: others are told to release Pharaoh toward killing, while Moses is released toward calling. The first action claims bodily reach; the second invokes rival lordship.

activation_trace.role: Leaving or releasing supplies the permission frame around Pharaoh's proposed action.
Lethal efficacy is Pharaoh's side of the staged contest.
Calling and drawing by speech supply Moses's counter-action.
Sovereign mastery identifies the power whose response Pharaoh implicitly challenges.
The effective speech of a ruler frames the whole scene as an attempted performative decree.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh dismissively permits Moses to pray while threatening him.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh scripts a public test between his own permission-dependent power to kill and Moses's call to a rival sovereign.

context_deltas.mechanism: Earlier context supplies a repeated sequence in which communities form an intention against a messenger, seize him, and twist argument in order to dislodge truth; the immediately preceding ayah supplies an actual killing policy. Pharaoh's preventive rationale now reads as the local wording of a recurrent coercive script.

activation_trace.role: The proposed taking of Moses's life anchors the recurring coercive mechanism in the focus.
An intention congealed within the self supplies the pre-action stage of the messenger-seizure pattern.
Capture and confinement connect the nations' attempted seizure of messengers with the answering seizure of the aggressors.
Twisted disputation supplies the rhetorical wrapping placed around coercion.
The attempted collapse of a proof supplies the declared argumentative aim behind seizure.
The preceding command to kill believers' sons makes lethal policy actual before Pharaoh individualizes it against Moses.

structural_cues: 40:5 orders intention, messenger-seizure, twisted dispute, attempted displacement of truth, and counter-seizure.
40:25 places an enacted collective killing command immediately before the focus's singular proposal.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the repeated sequence and the adjacent killing command; I infer that Pharaoh's announced fear rationalizes his place in that sequence. A materially live alternative is that he also experiences genuine political fear while reproducing the pattern.

changed_reading.before: The killing is an exceptional response to a new security threat.
changed_reading.after: The speech is a familiar messenger-seizure script in which preventive language and argumentative displacement prepare coercion.

context_deltas.mechanism: Moses immediately performs the supposedly permitted call as asylum in 'my Lord and your Lord,' undoing Pharaoh's possessive distancing. A concealed believer then states the present charge directly: killing a man for saying 'my Lord is God.' The feared future disruption is revised into hostility toward an already spoken transfer of lordship.

activation_trace.role: The permitted call anchors the response that the next ayah performs.
Moses's apparently private sovereign is the relation the context universalizes.
Seeking refuge and attachment turns calling into an effective jurisdictional appeal.
Mastery shared by 'my' and 'your' Lord breaks Pharaoh's attempt to isolate Moses's patron.
The day of account supplies the superior jurisdiction denied by the arrogant threat.
Concealment of faith creates an internal witness whose disclosure counters Pharaoh's public rationale.
The believer repeats literal killing as the act that needs justification.
Speech as professed belief identifies the utterance of lordship as the immediate ground of persecution.

structural_cues: 40:27 directly follows Pharaoh's 'let him call' with Moses's first-person refuge formula.
40:28 converts Pharaoh's projected future harms into the believer's present causal question: killing because a man says who his Lord is.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the immediate call, the pronoun expansion, and the believer's causal challenge; I infer that these expose allegiance as the operative charge. An alternative is that the believer strategically narrows a genuinely broader security case.

changed_reading.before: Moses may appeal to a private Lord after Pharaoh acts for public safety.
changed_reading.after: Moses invokes the Lord of both parties as a higher asylum, and the next speaker exposes confession of that lordship as the present reason for the threatened killing.

context_deltas.mechanism: The believing man repeats Pharaoh's exact posture of fearing 'for you,' but grounds it in patterned historical consequences and the day of mutual calling. Fear becomes a contested claim to protective care rather than transparent evidence of motive.

activation_trace.role: Pharaoh's expectation of harm anchors the first protective claim.
The believer reuses anticipated harm to make a rival claim of concern for the same audience.
An exemplary warning gives the believer's fear a historical evidentiary mechanism.
A severe event shifts the feared harm from regime change to consequence.
Repetition stabilizes the believer's counter-fear as a sustained protective stance.
Raised calling makes the feared day a public field of answering voices, countering Pharaoh's control of who may call.

structural_cues: 40:30 and 40:32 repeat the focus's first-person fear construction in the mouth of the concealed believer.
The believer's fear points backward to repeated peoples and forward to judgment, whereas Pharaoh's points toward suppressing Moses.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies parallel fear speeches with different objects and remedies; I infer that the parallel invites evaluation of fear by its causal warrant and proposed action. Both speakers could still be sincere at the affective level.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh's fear straightforwardly authenticates his concern for the people.
changed_reading.after: Fear is rival political-pastoral rhetoric: Pharaoh's fear authorizes killing, while the believer's fear authorizes warning through historical analogy.

context_deltas.mechanism: Whole-surah visibility repeatedly moves from concealed interiors to compulsory exposure. The court itself is described as dominant in the land, Pharaoh claims exclusive control of what he shows, and pride is located in breasts. The focus's 'make corruption appear' can therefore expose the dominant regime's hidden source of action even while retaining the reading 'make corruption prevail.'

activation_trace.role: Disclosure anchors the possibility that Moses makes a concealed condition publicly legible.
Loss of soundness is the condition whose true location is reopened by the context.
Universal emergence into exposure establishes the surah's terminal visibility horizon.
Hidden content supplies the interior counterpart to what the focus says may be made visible.
The breast as the source from which acts issue relocates causation beneath public claims.
Concealed faith demonstrates that the court's visible consensus contains a hidden counter-position.
The court's current dominance in the land activates the political-prevalence branch of the focus verb.
Pharaoh's claim that he only shows what he sees makes visibility itself an instrument of rule.
Pride magnified within the breast supplies a concealed motive beneath public disputation.

structural_cues: 40:16 and 40:19 pair total exposure with knowledge of concealed interiors.
40:29 places the same ظهر root in 'dominant in the land' and follows it with Pharaoh's monopoly claim over showing and seeing.
40:28 and 40:56 locate opposed hidden contents inside the regime: concealed faith and concealed pride.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the disclosure lexicon, the regime's visible dominance, and hidden interiors; I infer that Moses's feared act may reveal the regime's own corruption. The alternative that Pharaoh means only the future prevalence of Moses-caused disorder remains fully live.

changed_reading.before: The visible danger is corruption generated by Moses outside the regime.
changed_reading.after: Visibility is contested political control: Moses may make disorder prevail, but he may instead expose the hidden corruption of the order already dominant in the land.

context_deltas.mechanism: After daring Moses to call his Lord, Pharaoh orders a high structure, seeks a chain of means to reach and inspect Moses's God, then declares Moses a liar. The verbal challenge becomes an attempted surveillance and containment of rival lordship within Pharaoh's own vertical apparatus.

activation_trace.role: Moses's call anchors the rival relation Pharaoh later tries to inspect.
The called sovereign is converted by Pharaoh into an alleged object at the end of a built route.
A high construction supplies the material instrument of Pharaoh's counter-inquiry.
Reaching an endpoint supplies the assumed arrow from architecture to access.
A rope or connecting means turns the heavens into a traversable chain in Pharaoh's model.
Overlooking and uncovering an affair supply the surveillance goal.
Uncertain supposition reveals that the inquiry begins from a conclusion it claims to verify.
Loss and ruin mark the failure of the apparatus that sought to contain the call.

structural_cues: 40:36-37 follows the focus with a command to build, a vertical reach, an attempted look toward Moses's God, and a prior declaration of falsehood.
The same speaker who permits the call then tries to make its addressee available to his own visual regime.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the call, tower, chain of means, inspection, and declared suspicion; I infer a counter-call mechanism in which Pharaoh tries to domesticate rival lordship through surveillance. The tower may alternatively be pure public spectacle rather than sincere inquiry.

changed_reading.before: Letting Moses call is a disposable taunt.
changed_reading.after: The taunt initiates Pharaoh's failed attempt to bring the called Lord within an architecture of reach, sight, and official verification.

context_deltas.mechanism: Later calls are explicitly directional: the believer calls toward rescue while his people call toward fire, then entrusts his affair to God. God finally commands 'call Me' and supplies the missing response, while refusal is tied to pride against service. Pharaoh's challenge to Moses's call is answered by a surah-wide invitation-response system.

activation_trace.role: The focus call anchors the efficacy question later calls resolve.
The challenged Lord is the speaker who later invites and answers calling.
Opposed vocal invitations supply two destinations and make calling socially directional.
Rescue as separation supplies the destination of the believer's counter-call.
Entrusting the affair to another supplies the operational completion of appeal to higher authority.
The direct invitation to call removes Pharaoh's assumed control over whether the appeal may occur.
Answering speech supplies the explicit efficacy that Pharaoh's dare leaves in question.
Submissive service joins call-response to the allegiance contested in 'your din.'

structural_cues: 40:41-44 develops repeated calls with opposed destinations and ends in entrusting the affair to God.
40:60 places call and answer in immediate verbal sequence, then identifies pride against service as the refusal mechanism.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies opposed calls, entrustment, and an explicit divine answer; I infer that these retrospectively answer Pharaoh's efficacy challenge. The focus may still portray Pharaoh as merely contemptuous rather than consciously testing a response.

changed_reading.before: Moses's call is an impotent accompaniment to Pharaoh's lethal action.
changed_reading.after: Calling is the surah's directional and responsive mechanism: it moves people toward rival ends, transfers an affair, and receives an answer from the Lord Pharaoh challenges.

context_deltas.mechanism: Pharaoh says of Moses, 'let him call his Lord.' Later those in the fire ask the keepers, 'call your Lord' to reduce one day of punishment, and are told to call for themselves, but their call is lost. The same possessive distancing and delegated appeal return against Pharaoh's side.

activation_trace.role: The third-person appeal supplies the wording later mirrored by the condemned speakers.
The distancing possessive 'his Lord' anchors the reversal to 'your Lord.'
A delegated call repeats Pharaoh's grammar from the position of need.
Calling the keepers' master 'your Lord' preserves the earlier refusal to own the relation.
Reduction in amount supplies the minimal relief now sought from the once-dismissed authority.
The command to call and the failed calling of disbelievers complete the reversal.
Loss makes the late delegated call fail to arrive at the relief it seeks.

structural_cues: 40:49 reproduces the focus's call-plus-possessive-Lord construction with changed pronouns and reversed power.
40:50 answers the delegation by returning the imperative to the speakers and declaring the disbelievers' call lost.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the close grammatical mirror and its failed outcome; I infer deliberate temporal reversal of Pharaoh's dare. The later speakers are a broader condemned collective, so identification with Pharaoh's immediate court remains narrative rather than one-to-one.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh can distance himself from Moses's Lord and leave Moses alone to call.
changed_reading.after: That distancing grammar returns from the position of helplessness: Pharaoh's side delegates a call to another's Lord and discovers that the refused relation cannot be outsourced at the end.

context_deltas.mechanism: The surah brackets Pharaoh's 'your din' with commands to make din exclusive for God, narrates guidance and the Book passing by inheritance to Israel, and commands submission to the Lord of the worlds. Din is removed from Pharaoh's possessive custody and recast as exclusive allegiance that can outlive coercion through transmitted guidance.

activation_trace.role: Replacement anchors Pharaoh's fear that one normative order will stand where another stood.
Obedience and worship supply the relation being reassigned.
Exclusive separation from association removes din from mixed or partisan ownership.
Din as obedient worship is explicitly directed to God before Pharaoh calls it 'yours.'
Transmission of knowledge or Book by inheritance supplies a noncoercive mechanism of normative succession.
Gentle guidance toward the right path names what survives Pharaoh's attempted suppression.
A written fixing that establishes judgment gives inherited guidance durable normative form.
The repeated exclusive din confirms that allegiance is God's rather than a ruler's possession.
Handing oneself over supplies the enacted posture toward the Lord of the worlds.

structural_cues: 40:14 precedes the focus with din made exclusive for God; 40:65 repeats the formula after the Pharaoh narrative.
40:53 places Moses, guidance, Israelite inheritance, and the Book in one succession statement.
40:66 opposes worship of what the audience calls to submission to the Lord of all worlds.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies exclusive din, inherited guidance, and commanded submission; I infer that these de-possess Pharaoh's 'your din' and narrate the feared change as durable succession. The inheritance verse need not denote a direct administrative replacement of Egypt's order.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh protects a community-owned religion from unauthorized alteration.
changed_reading.after: His possessive formula tries to hold allegiance in place, while the surah assigns din exclusively to God and shows guidance surviving as inherited written order.

context_deltas.mechanism: Pharaoh's royal speech proposes death but first asks others to release him and later fails. Divine speech gives life and death, issues a decisive affair, says 'be,' and the event occurs; messengers themselves bring signs only by divine permission. The efficacy contest is resolved by relocating command, authorization, and realization.

activation_trace.role: The ruler's consequential speech anchors the attempted human decree.
The request to be released reveals that Pharaoh's action remains socially mediated.
Taking life is the efficacy Pharaoh claims for his speech.
Removing life places the power Pharaoh claims within the divine subject's scope.
A decisive judgment or command supplies finality without Pharaoh's deliberative permission scene.
Binding command identifies the affair whose realization follows speech.
Uttered saying supplies the verbal act immediately paired with realization.
Occurrence and presence in time supply the event that answers the command without delay.
Authorization limits even a messenger's sign to divine permission, clarifying the hierarchy of effective agency.

structural_cues: The focus sequences Pharaoh's saying, request for release, intended killing, and Moses's call.
40:68 compresses divine life, death, decision, saying, and occurrence into one causal sequence.
40:78 explicitly places messenger-signs under permission and final judgment under God's command.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies contrasting speech-action sequences and explicit authorization; I infer that the later sequence resolves the focus's sovereignty test. The theological contrast does not erase the real delegated violence available to Pharaoh in the immediate scene.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh's command controls death, while Moses can only speak upward.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh's lethal decree is mediated and frustrated; life, death, authorization, decisive command, and self-realizing speech belong to the Lord Moses calls.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is surprising because financial debt is not the ordinary local rendering of din, but it remains anchored in the packet's din branches and is activated by the surah's earned recompense, debt-collection image, and repeated account. Downstream prose should present it as a jurisdictional ledger analogy, not as a replacement translation.

activation_trace.role: Judgment and recompense make din an accountability regime as well as confession.
Financial debt supplies the exploratory ledger image for obligations owed under a ruler.
Collecting and satisfying a debt makes recompense function like settlement of an account.
Acquired earnings supply what is entered on the moral ledger.
Counting and account supply the reckoning that closes the ledger.
Disbelief in the day of account connects Pharaoh's arrogant order to refusal of superior settlement.

changed_reading.before: Moses may replace a set of beliefs.
changed_reading.after: Exploratorily, Pharaoh fears that Moses will change the ledger of obligation: who is obeyed, what is owed, and before whose account actions are finally settled.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is a deliberately cross-domain material analogy built from peripheral earth branches: wood-boring consumption and a suppurating lesion. It remains valid because both branches attach directly to الأرض beside يظهر and الفساد, while the context repeatedly exposes hidden interiors. It should be rendered only as an exploratory image of internal decay, never as the lexical meaning of الأرض.

activation_trace.role: Disclosure supplies the movement from concealed decay to visible condition.
A wood-borer consuming material from within supplies one contained image for latent civic decay.
An ulcer spoiled by collected matter supplies a second image for corruption becoming externally legible.
Departure from soundness is the shared condition linking the material analogy to the focus.
Concealment supplies the hidden phase before exposure.
The interior source from which acts issue makes the body-politic analogy causally coherent.

changed_reading.before: Moses imports an external disorder into an otherwise sound land.
changed_reading.after: As a contained material analogy, Moses may expose corruption already eating or suppurating within the land's political body.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: The root branch 'complete mastery in knowledge' is form-distant from the unequivocally lethal syntax and cannot displace literal killing, which nearby ayat reinforce. It remains worth carrying because Pharaoh later builds an apparatus to inspect and settle Moses's claim. Downstream prose should treat it as a secondary motive-layer coupling elimination with attempted epistemic capture.

activation_trace.role: Complete epistemic mastery supplies the exploratory sense of settling Moses's claim by conquering it.
The high structure materializes an apparatus for mastering the rival claim.
Reaching the endpoint supplies the assumption that the claim can be exhaustively accessed.
Inspection and uncovering supply the knowledge operation that accompanies coercion.
Supposition and doubt show the unresolved claim Pharaoh seeks to close while already calling it false.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh seeks only Moses's bodily death.
changed_reading.after: Without weakening the literal threat, the killing proposal also carries an exploratory drive to master, settle, and close Moses's claim through coercive knowledge.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This activation uses the packet's non-dominant split mapping from دعو to دعع, so it is intentionally branch-distant. It remains anchored because the focus call is syntactically paired with Pharaoh's force and later calls explicitly direct people toward rescue or fire. Render it only as a force-vector metaphor, never as a lexical substitution for 'call.'

activation_trace.role: A forceful push supplies the exploratory image of the call exerting counter-pressure against Pharaoh's decree.
Lethal force supplies the opposed vector with which the call is paired.
Opposed calls toward rescue and fire make speech function as social propulsion.
Rescue by separation supplies one destination toward which the counter-force moves.
The answering return supplies the reciprocal motion that completes the call.

changed_reading.before: Moses's call is passive speech beside Pharaoh's physical force.
changed_reading.after: As a contained split-root metaphor, the call is a counter-force that redirects allegiance and receives an answering return.

strongest_changes: The alleged future security threat becomes a recurrent messenger-seizure script and is immediately exposed as hostility to a spoken transfer of lordship.
Moses answers 'let him call his Lord' by seeking refuge in 'my Lord and your Lord,' defeating Pharaoh's possessive distancing.
The believer's repeated 'I fear for you' turns fear into a contest between rival claims of protective care.
The visibility clause can turn back on the dominant regime: Moses may expose hidden corruption rather than originate it.
The surah answers Pharaoh's dare with call-and-response, then reverses his grammar when the condemned ask others to 'call your Lord' for them.
Pharaoh's mediated lethal decree is finally contrasted with divine life, death, authorization, decisive command, and self-realizing speech.
summary.what_was_special: The whole-surah packet made one compact speech recur as a network of pronoun reversals, rival fear claims, visibility controls, delegated calls, and competing speech-action systems. The most diagnostic activation was not a new topic but the return of Pharaoh's own wording from positions he could not control.
remaining_uncertainties: The focus verb يظهر still supports both disclosure and political prevalence; context strengthens both rather than disambiguating them.
Pharaoh's fear may be affectively sincere even if the narrative pattern makes it a coercive rationale.
The tower may be a sincere but category-bound inquiry, a public spectacle, or both.
The obligation-ledger, internal-rot, epistemic-capture, and split-root force readings are exploratory analogies and must not replace the dominant lexical senses.

reader_a.activated_readings_md:
1. **The ruler projects replacement onto the messenger while proposing bodily removal.** `ب د ل/B001` gives one thing taking another’s place; `ق ت ل/B001` supplies killing. The feared substitution is answered by an attempted substitution of absence for presence. I infer that monopoly is preserved by removing the rival source; the speech reads as political self-disclosure.
2. **“Manifest corruption” can mean exposing what rule keeps latent.** `ظ ه ر/B001` supplies coming into view, while `ف س د/B001` gives departure from sound balance. Grammatically Pharaoh assigns Moses as cause; alternatively, I infer that public disclosure makes an existing disorder visible. Both readings remain: producing corruption and revealing systemic corruption.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: The tower in 40:36–37 confirms that Pharaoh’s fear of replacement generates its own rival program of manifestation, while 40:45 exposes where corruption settles.

reader_a.activated_readings_md: 1. **Killing is proposed as conservation of an order feared to be replaceable.** Lexically, `ب د ل:B001` is "replacement or substitution," `ظ ه ر:B001` is coming out into view, and `ف س د:B001` is departure from soundness and balance. Structurally, Pharaoh links removing one speaker to preventing a replacement of `دينكم` or a public emergence; in 40:28, concealed faith from his own house comes into speech. Replacement plays the feared systemic role, while killing is cast as a blocking operation. The packet gives this proposed means and the next hidden believer; I infer Pharaoh assumes suppression of the messenger will preserve the existing order. The ayah reads as anxious institutional maintenance, with the following emergence already exposing the plan's faulty causal model.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: Later 40:36-37 makes Pharaoh himself display corrupt work through the tower, while 40:45 surrounds his household; suppression produces the public failure it claimed to prevent.

baseline.text: Firavun dedi ki: Bırakın beni, Musa'yı öldüreyim; o da Rabbine yalvarsın. Sizin dininizi değiştirmesinden veya yeryüzünde bozgunculuk çıkarmasından korkuyorum.

findings.text: Firavun, düzeni değiştirme korkusuna Musa'nın bedenini yok ederek karşılık verir; böylece korumaya çalıştığı tekeli ve rakip kaynağı yoklukla değiştirme siyasetini açığa vurur.
Bozgunculuğu ortaya çıkarma ifadesi, Musa'nın yeni bir bozukluk üretmesi yanında yönetimin gizli dengesizliğini görünür kılması ihtimalini de taşır.

inter_ayah_rows.note: Pharaoh gathers his stratagem and appointed assembly against Moses, showing his opposition organized as public power.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The magicians' sudden belief in the Lord of Moses and Aaron explains the rupture that provokes Pharaoh's subsequent threat.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Pharaoh presents Moses to his chiefs as a learned magician, continuing the campaign to define the messenger as a public danger.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The chiefs repeat that Moses seeks to expel them from their land, a close political counterpart to the focus's allegation.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: When Moses brings clear signs, Pharaoh's circle calls them fabricated magic and denies precedent, supplying the rejection that precedes the threat.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The surah's account of Moses' mission with authority and clear proof begins the immediate narrative unit containing the focus.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The believer invokes the fate of earlier factions to rebut Pharaoh's course and extend the warning after the focus.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The believer recalls earlier persistent doubt and the killing of Joseph, placing Pharaoh's treatment of Moses in a recurrent history of rejecting messengers.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Pharaoh's order to build a tower so he can look upon Moses' God develops his attempt to replace response to signs with sovereign spectacle.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: His stated aim to disbelieve Moses and his beautified evil plan make explicit the denial concealed by his fear-for-religion rhetoric.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The believer contrasts Pharaoh's summons to disbelief and the Fire with his own summons to God, resolving the competing calls in the scene.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Pharaoh's belittling comparison of Moses to himself shows the social-status rhetoric used to prevent recognition of the messenger.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: His demand for material tokens of rank continues the public effort to disqualify Moses rather than answer his message.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Pharaoh manipulates his people into obedience, showing how his accusation against Moses functions through a compliant public.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The testing of Pharaoh's people by a noble messenger provides another compact framing of the same mission and rejection.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Moses' demand that they yield to God's servants directly conflicts with Pharaoh's claim to command the religious-political order.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Moses seeks refuge from their intended stoning, adding a direct threat of violence to the Pharaoh confrontation.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Moses is commanded to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, again reversing Pharaoh's portrayal of Moses as the danger.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Pharaoh's gathering and public call show his use of assembled power to sustain his challenge to Moses.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: The punishment of Pharaoh for his latter and former claim supplies the consequence for the authority asserted in the focus.

inter_ayah_rows.label: medium
inter_ayah_rows.note: Pharaoh calls Moses bewitched despite the clear signs, furnishing another instance of his counter-accusation against the messenger.

root_profile.summary: Bu kök, sesle söze dökme çekirdeğinden konuşma organı, konuşkan kişi, eski unvan, yalan isnat, söylenti, müzakere, hüküm dayatma, iç söz, görüş benimseme, sözsüz belirtme, içten önemseme, teknik tanım ve içe doğan anlam gibi ayrı dallara yayılır.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesi azlığı çokluğun karşıtı olarak verir; ayrıca yoksulluk, düşüklük, bir şeyi az görme ve belirli yapılarda yokluğa ya da seyrekliğe yaklaşan kullanımları açıkça destekler.
identity_judgment.boundary_note: Bu kol yalnızca sayı ve miktar azlığını ve buna bağlı kullanımları kapsar; yükseklik, kap, taşıma ve titreme anlamlarını kapsamaz.

lexicalization_scope.note: Temel azlık anlamı ile yoksullaşma ve az görme gibi türemiş biçimler birlikte bulunur; yokluk ve seyrekleşme anlamları ise yalnızca belirtilen yapılara bağlıdır.

concept_map.definition: Bir şeyin sayı, miktar ya da ölçü bakımından çok olmayışını bildirir. Bundan yoksulluk ve düşüklük, bir şeyi az sayma veya az gösterme ve belirli yapılarda hiçlik ya da seyrek gerçekleşme anlamları gelişir.

facets.statement: Bir varlığın sayı, miktar veya ölçü bakımından çok olmayışıdır.
Azlık, kişinin yoksullaşması veya toplum içinde düşük ve değersiz görülmesi sonucuna uzanabilir.
Bir şeyi gerçekte ya da değerlendiren kişinin gözünde az sayma ve az gösterme anlamını taşır.
Belirli olumsuzluk ve sıklık yapılarında hiç yokluğu veya bir eylemin pek seyrek gerçekleşmesini anlatır.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Tanımlar azlığın temel sayı ve miktar karşıtlığında birleşir; yoksulluk ve düşüklük, az sayma ve bazı yapılarda yokluğa yaklaşan kullanım bu çekirdeğin düzenli uzantılarıdır.

concept_gloss.applicability: Sayı, miktar veya ölçünün çok olmayışını bildiren temel anlam için uygundur.

error_profile.preserves: Çokluğun karşıtı olan sayı ve miktar azlığını doğrudan korur.

contextual_glosses.applicability: Bir şeyin sayı veya miktar bakımından çok olmadığının söylendiği bağlamlarda kullanılır.

error_profile.preserves: Temel azlık durumunu doğal bir Türkçe yapıyla tam olarak verir.

contextual_glosses.applicability: Azlığın kişide yoksulluk ve toplumsal düşüklük sonucu doğurduğu bağlamlara özgüdür.

error_profile.preserves: Yoksulluk ile düşüklük arasındaki kaynakta kurulan uzantıyı korur.

contextual_glosses.applicability: Bir miktarın veya verilen bir şeyin yetersiz ya da küçük sayıldığı değerlendirme bağlamlarında kullanılır.

contextual_glosses.applicability: Yalnızca sıklığı çok düşüren veya olumsuzluğu pekiştiren kalıplaşmış yapılarda kullanılır.

branches.neighbor_coverage_note: Bütün adaylar karşılaştırıldı; genel azlıkla en yakın örtüşme, değersizlikle kurulan yan ilişki ve aynı kökteki tepe anlamıyla olası karışma en açıklayıcı üç sınır olarak seçildi.
branches.what_is_ar: القليل والقِلَّة ضد الكثرة، ويدخل فيه الافتقار والذلة، وتقليل الشيء في العين، واستقلاله، واستعمال القليل للنفي أو للندرة
branches.what_is_not_ar: ليس علو الشيء ولا الجرة ولا الحمل ولا الرعدة
branches.source_phrase_ar: القل القليل؛ رماه الله بالقل والذل أي بالقلة والذلة (jamhara)؛ شيء قليل وجمعه قلل؛ قل الشيء يقل قلة؛ قلله في عينه؛ أقل افتقر؛ استقله عده قليلا (sihah)؛ قل الشيء يقل قلة فهو قليل وقلال؛ القل من الرجال الخسيس الدنيء؛ قليلة ولا كثيرة؛ قليلا ما يؤمنون؛ قاللت لفلان؛ تقاللت ما أعطاني (tahdhib)؛ القلة والكثرة يستعملان في الأعداد؛ يكنى بالقلة عن الذلة؛ يكنى بها تارة عن العزة؛ قليل يعبر به عن النفي (mufradat)

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesi bir şeyin en üstünü veya başını çekirdek anlam olarak verir; dağın yuvarlak üst bölümü, insan başı ve kılıcın başındaki topuz bu çekirdeğin açık uzmanlaşmalarıdır.
identity_judgment.boundary_note: Bu kol uzamsal başı ve en üst parçayı bildirir; sayısal azlık ya da büyük kap anlamını içermez.

lexicalization_scope.note: Genel baş ve en üst bölüm anlamı ile dağ tepesi, insan başı ve kılıç topuzu gibi yapıya bağlı uzmanlaşmalar ayrı tutulur.

concept_map.definition: Bir şeyin başını veya en üst bölümünü bildirir. Dağın üstteki yuvarlak parçası, insan başı ve kılıcın sap ucundaki topuz bu uzamsal çekirdeğin özel gerçekleşmeleridir.

facets.statement: Bir nesnenin veya oluşumun başı ya da en üstte bulunan bölümüdür.
Dağın en üstünde yer alan, kimi tanımda yuvarlak biçimli bölümünü adlandırır.
İnsan başı ile kılıcın sap ucundaki başlık veya topuz da aynı üst ve baş kavramıyla adlandırılır.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Tanımlar bir şeyin başı ve en üst bölümü üzerinde birleşir; dağ tepesi temel örnektir, insan başı ile kılıç topuzu da aynı biçimsel ve uzamsal çizgide yer alır.

concept_gloss.applicability: Bir nesnenin ya da doğal oluşumun en üst bölümünü ve başını kapsayan genel karşılıktır.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesi büyük bir küp veya iri kap anlamında birleşir; iki kaplık ölçü ve belirli bir bölgeyle anılan iri küpler de aynı kap anlamını somutlaştırır.
identity_judgment.boundary_note: Bu kol büyük bir kap türünü ve onun ölçü değerini kapsar; nicelik azlığı veya dağ tepesi anlamını kapsamaz.

lexicalization_scope.note: Büyük küp anlamı çekirdektir; belirli bir bölgeye bağlanan kap adı ile iki kaplık ölçü yalnızca kendi yapılardaki uzmanlaşmalardır.

concept_map.definition: Büyük bir küpü veya küpe benzeyen iri kabı bildirir. Belirli bir bölgenin iri küpleri ve iki böyle kabın aldığı miktar bu kap anlamına bağlı özel kullanımlardır.

facets.statement: Küpe benzeyen, özellikle sıvı taşımaya veya saklamaya elverişli büyük bir kaptır.
Belirli bir bölgeyle anılan iri küpler veya büyük toprak kaplar bu adın tanınmış bir türünü oluşturur.
İki büyük kap, bu iki kabın kendisini veya onların aldığı sıvı miktarını bildiren bir ölçü değeri kazanır.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Tanımlar iri bir küp veya büyük kap üzerinde birleşir; tanınmış bölgesel kaplar büyüklüğü örnekler, iki kaplık kullanım ise nesne adını kapasite ölçüsüne taşır.

concept_gloss.applicability: Küpe benzeyen iri kabı adlandıran temel ve en doğal Türkçe karşılıktır.

error_profile.preserves: Kabın küp türünde ve olağandan büyük oluşunu birlikte korur.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesi yükü taşıma veya taşıyabilme ile öznenin yükselip harekete geçmesini aynı kolda açıkça toplar; kuşun uçuşa kalkması, göğün yükselmesi ve yolcuların yüklenip ayrılması ayrı katılımcı gerçekleşmeleridir.
identity_judgment.boundary_note: Taşıma, yükselme ve yüklenerek yola koyulma bu kolun sınırıdır; salt sayısal azlık bu anlamlara katılmaz.

lexicalization_scope.note: Yük taşıma ile yükselme çekirdek çizgileri ayrılır; ağır bulut taşıma, uçuşa kalkma ve yolcuların ayrılması yalnızca kendi özne ve yapılarında geçerlidir.

concept_map.definition: Bir yükü kaldırıp taşıyabilmeyi veya üstlenmeyi ve bir öznenin yükselerek harekete geçmesini bildirir. İkinci çizgi kuşun uçuşa kalkmasını, göğün yükselmesini ve yolcuların yüklenip yola koyulmasını kapsar.

facets.statement: Bir nesneyi kaldıracak gücü bulmak, onu taşımak veya yük olarak üstlenmektir.
Bir öznenin aşağıdaki konumundan yükselmesi veya kuş gibi harekete ve uçuşa başlamasıdır.
Yolcuların yüklerini alıp bulundukları yerden ayrılarak yolculuğa başlamasıdır.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Tanımlar bir yükü kaldırıp taşıma ile yukarı kalkarak harekete geçme çizgilerini bir araya getirir; kuş, gök, bulut ve yolcu örnekleri katılımcıya göre bu iki çizgiyi somutlaştırır.

concept_gloss.text: yük kaldırma, yükselme ve yola koyulma
concept_gloss.applicability: Taşıma, yukarı kalkma ve yüklenerek hareket etme çizgilerinin birlikte özetlenmesi gereken kavram haritasında kullanılır.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesinin baskın anlamı ayrı bir et parçasıdır. Bunun yanında tek bir aktarım etsiz bir kemik parçasından söz eder; ayrıca çok sayıda et parçası içeren yemek kullanımı, adın temel anlamını değiştirmeyen yapıya bağlı bir uygulamadır.
identity_judgment.boundary_note: Temel ad anlamı et parçasıyla sınırlıdır; etsiz kemik açıklaması bir kaynak ayrılığı, yemek örneği ise yapıya bağlı kullanımdır.

lexicalization_scope.note: Tanım, bağımsız adın et ya da aktarıma göre kemik parçası anlamını, bol et parçalı yemek yapısından ayrı tutar.

concept_map.definition: Başlıca anlamı bütünden ayrılmış bir et parçasıdır; bir aktarımda bunun yerine üzerinde et bulunmayan bir kemik parçası gösterilir. Çoğul nitelikli kullanım, bir ekmek yemeğinde çok sayıda et parçası bulunmasını anlatır.

facets.statement: Bütünden ayrılmış tek bir et parçasını adlandırır.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Kaynakların ortak ağırlığı et parçası anlamındadır. Toplu kanıt ayrıca etsiz kemik parçası yorumunu ve çok sayıda et parçası içeren yemek kullanımını kaydeder; bunlar temel ad anlamıyla aynı düzlemde genelleştirilmemelidir.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesinin çekirdeği bir şeyi bırakmak ya da kendi haline koymaktır. Ancak kullanım geçmiş zaman ve bağımsız eylem adı yerine geniş zaman ile emir biçimlerinde yaşar; değersiz görülen şeyi bir yana atma yorumu da çekirdeğe bağlı özel bir uzantıdır.
identity_judgment.boundary_note: Bırakma anlamı korunmalı, sınırlı çekim düzeni ve küçümseyerek bir yana atma uzantısı ayrıca belirtilmelidir.

lexicalization_scope.note: Tanım, geniş zaman ve emir biçimlerindeki bırakma çekirdeğini, belirli nesneli yapıları ve küçümseyerek atma uzantısını ayırır.

concept_map.definition: Bir şeyi olduğu yerde ya da kendi halinde bırakmak, onunla ilgilenmekten vazgeçmektir. Kullanım geniş zaman ve emir biçimlerinde sürer; değersiz görülen bir şeyi bir yana atma anlamına da uzanabilir.

facets.statement: Bir şeyi bırakmayı veya kendi haline koymayı belirtir.
Eylem geniş zaman ve emir biçimlerinde kullanılır; geçmiş zaman biçimi ile bağımsız eylem adı kullanım dışıdır.
Değersiz görülen bir şeyi önemsemeyerek bir yana atmayı anlatabilir.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Toplu kanıt bırakma ve kendi haline koyma çekirdeğinde birleşir; kullanımın geniş zaman ve emir biçimleriyle sınırlı olduğunu, eylem adının başka bir bırakma sözüyle anlatıldığını ve küçümseyerek bir yana atma uzantısını da kaydeder.

concept_gloss.applicability: Dalın temel bırakma anlamı, özel çekim biçimlerinden bağımsız olarak kısa biçimde gösterileceğinde kullanılır.

error_profile.preserves: Nesneyle ilgiyi kesip onu kendi halinde bırakma çekirdeğini korur.

contextual_glosses.applicability: Bırakma eyleminin doğrudan emir biçiminde söylendiği bağlamlarda kullanılır.

error_profile.preserves: Emir biçimini ve nesneyi kendi halinde bırakma anlamını korur.

contextual_glosses.applicability: Bırakmanın, nesneye az değer verme nedeniyle onu atma biçiminde gerçekleştiği bağlamlarda kullanılır.

error_profile.preserves: Az değer verme gerekçesini ve bir yana atma sonucunu korur.

lexical_glosses.target_gloss: önemsiz gördüğü şeyi bir yana atmak

error_profile.preserves: Bir şeyle ilgilenmeme sonucunu kısmen korur.
error_profile.loses: Bir şeyi bilinçli olarak bırakma ya da kendi haline koyma işlemini kaybeder.
error_profile.adds: Bellekten silinme veya hatırlayamama anlamını ekler.
error_profile.collision: Bırakma eylemini zihinsel bir başarısızlıkla karıştırır.

neighbor_distinctions.neighbor_only: Komşu dal terk etme, salıverme, ilgisiz bırakma ve hayvan ya da malı engellemeden koyma gibi daha geniş kullanımlara sahiptir.

neighbor_distinctions.shared_zone: Her iki dal da bir şeyi almama, sürdürmeme veya kendi haline bırakma bağlamında kullanılabilir.
neighbor_distinctions.distinction: Komşu dal niyet ve zorunluluk bakımından daha geniş bir bırakma alanı kurar; odak dal ise anlamca yakın olmakla birlikte biçimsel olarak sınırlıdır.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesi, sabit bir sesleniş kalıbının sövme ve yüz kızartıcı suçlama amacıyla kullanıldığını açıkça gösterir. Cinsel gönderimin açıklaması erkek cinsel organları ile sünnet derisi arasında değişir; ilgili ad biçiminin klitoris anlamı ise bu kalıptan ayrı tutulmalıdır.
identity_judgment.boundary_note: Sabit sövgü kalıbı ile bağımsız adın anatomik anlamı ayrılmalı, cinsel gönderimin değişken açıklaması tek bir organa indirgenmemelidir.

lexicalization_scope.note: Tanım, cinsel göndermeli sabit sövgü kalıplarını bağımsız ad biçiminin klitoris anlamından açıkça ayırır.

concept_map.definition: Sabit bir sesleniş kalıbında, cinsel organlara üstü kapalı gönderme yoluyla kişiye ve soyuna yöneltilen ağır bir sövgüdür; gönderimin erkek cinsel organları ya da sünnet derisi olduğu açıklanır. Bundan ayrı olarak ilgili ad biçimi klitorisi adlandırır.

facets.statement: Sabit bir sesleniş kalıbı, kişiye ve soyuna yöneltilen ağır sövgü ve yüz kızartıcı suçlama işlevi görür.
Kalıptaki cinsel gönderim erkek cinsel organları ya da sünnet derisi olarak farklı biçimlerde açıklanır.
Sövgü kalıbından ayrı olan ilgili ad biçimi kadın klitorisini adlandırır.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Toplu kanıt sabit kalıbın ağır sövgü ve yüz kızartıcı suçlama işlevinde birleşir. Cinsel imanın hangi anatomik öğeye dayandığı konusunda erkek cinsel organları ile sünnet derisi açıklamaları bulunur; ayrıca bağımsız ad biçimi klitoris için kaydedilir.
